Three Bike Trips and a Missing Day

Pittsburgh to DC, Montréal to Québec City and back, and a rail trail across Washington

TLDR: I have done three multi-day bike trips in the last four summers — {{TOTAL_MILES}} recorded miles over {{TOTAL_DAYS}} days of riding — and all three were worth doing. The flat one was the easiest, the paved one was the longest, and the windy one made the best story.

I keep a note called “Bike Trips” with five lines in it. Two of them never left a GPS trail I can find, so this is about the other three: the Great Allegheny Passage and C&O Canal from Pittsburgh to DC in 2023, the Route Verte from Montréal to Québec City and back in 2025, and the Palouse to Cascades trail east of Seattle this past June.

I didn’t set out with a list of requirements, but looking at the three together the pattern is pretty clear:

  1. No cars. All three are rail trails, towpaths or signed bike routes. I’ll take worse gravel over a better shoulder.
  2. Four or five days. Each trip is wrapped around a holiday weekend: the Fourth of July once and Juneteenth twice. That is about as much vacation as I want to spend sitting on a bike seat.
  3. A town with a burger and a beer at the end of most days. This one is not negotiable.

Twelve days, drawn to the same scale

The trips got harder in a different way each time. Pittsburgh to DC is long but flat, and the hard part is one climb. Québec was four days of roughly a hundred miles each, which is a lot of hours even when the pavement is good. Washington had the shortest days on paper and the slowest one in practice.

Strava, for its part, was not paying attention. Of the twelve rides, seven are titled “Evening Ride” or “Night Ride,” including two that left before nine in the morning. The one that left Québec City at 9:00 am is filed as a Night Ride, which after thirteen hours and twenty minutes was at least accurate by the end.

Pittsburgh to DC, July 2023

{{TABLE_GAP}}

The route. The Great Allegheny Passage runs about 150 miles from Pittsburgh to Cumberland, Maryland, and the C&O Canal towpath picks up there and runs another 185 or so into Georgetown. It is the standard first bike trip on the East Coast for a reason: you can’t get lost, and nothing on it is steep.

What the log says. I left Pittsburgh after noon on July 1 and did 61 miles. Day two was the big one: 93 miles and 3,850 feet of climbing, which is the long drag up to the Eastern Continental Divide and the drop into Cumberland. After that the towpath is as flat as a canal, because it is one. The last two recorded days total 132 miles and 291 feet of climbing between them.

The missing day. There is no ride on July 3. The ride on the 2nd ends about where Cumberland is and the ride on the 4th starts in Hancock, sixty-odd miles down the canal, so I didn’t teleport. I just didn’t press the button.That puts the real total around 345 miles against the 286 Strava has. If it isn’t on Strava it didn’t happen, except that my legs were there. My camera roll has four photos from that evening, all taken inside a minute, so I was definitely somewhere.

The gripe. The schedule, which was my own doing. Leaving Pittsburgh after noon is what turned day two into 93 miles with all of the trip’s climbing in it. By the last day I was averaging 11.6 miles an hour on dead-flat ground, the slowest of the trip, and was fine with that.

Montréal to Québec City and back, June 2025

{{TABLE_VERTE}}

The route. The Route Verte is Québec’s province-wide bike network. I went out along the north shore of the St. Lawrence through Trois-Rivières and came back along the south shore through Nicolet, so the river was on the same side the whole way and I never rode the same road twice.

What the log says. This is the big-mileage trip: 397 miles in four days, 34 hours of moving time, and no day under 87 miles. The first two days were in the rain. Day two into Québec City was 61 degrees and wet, and it is also where the climbing shows up: about 2,000 feet, after 589 the day before.

The gripe. The way home. Day three took 13 hours and 20 minutes door to door for 104 miles. Day four was 99 miles into a 15 mile-an-hour wind out of the west-southwest, which is the exact direction Montréal is in. It was my slowest day of the trip at 10.8 miles an hour, and I got in after nine at night.

Would I change it? If I did it again I’d look hard at five days. The same route is 79 miles a day instead of 99, and a hundred miles a day turns a trip into a job with a commute.

Palouse to Cascades, June 2026

{{TABLE_P2C}}

The route. The Palouse to Cascades trail is an old Milwaukee Road rail bed that crosses Washington. Everyone still calls it the John Wayne Trail, including my own notes. We rode it out and back from North Bend: over Snoqualmie Pass, down through Cle Elum and Ellensburg, across the Army’s Yakima Training Center to the Columbia River, and home the same way. We never actually reached the Palouse.

Getting there. We flew into Seattle and rented bikes from a shop in North Bend: Niners with 43mm tires. I wished for wider but you take what you can get, and the bikes were great. The first speed bump was the trailhead shuttle that Seattle runs in the summer, which we had planned on and which turns out to run on weekends only. It was a Thursday. We threw some capital at the problem, and $200 later an Uber XXL was hauling us to North Bend.The better deal of the trip: a hostel next to Pike Place stored our extra bags for $5 a day each, without us being guests. Every other option we priced was worse.

Day one, North Bend to Ponderosa Pines. 74 miles. We underestimated the climb. It is a rail grade and never steep, but it is about 30 miles of uphill without a break before you reach the Snoqualmie Tunnel, and we had started at 11. The tunnel is more than two miles long and unlit. Turn your lights off halfway through and stand in the dark for a minute. There is no real lunch for the first 40 miles, so ours was a late burger in Easton. In Cle Elum we strapped a 12-pack to a rack and rode it out to the campground, where it doesn’t get dark until after ten, and we stayed up far too late.

Day two, Ponderosa Pines to Vantage. 61 miles. The forest turns into farmland and then into high desert. Cherries at the Thorp fruit stand, lunch in Ellensburg at a place right on the trail, water and snacks in Kittitas. After the Renslow trestle there is nothing for 20 miles: no water, no shade, soft sand in some stretches and chunky rock in others. There is a water pump at Doris, and turning it on made us feel like roughnecks on an oil rig. Then it is downhill to the river at Beverly and nine miles of pavement to Vantage, where the RV park had showers.

Day three, back the way we came. 61 miles, and the orange bar in the chart. The wind blew 35 miles an hour or better all night and nobody slept. We broke camp in the mood of soldiers going to war who know they might not make it home. Then we climbed back onto the training grounds into that same wind, on the same sand: 8 hours 13 minutes of pedaling at 7.4 miles an hour, and nearly 13 hours out the door. The headwind held all the way through Ellensburg and didn’t let up until the trees past Thorp. The one bright spot was a cheesesteak in Kittitas, made by an actual Philadelphian.

Day four, the payoff. 64 miles, and the bikes were due back by four. This is where the first day’s climb pays you back: from the tunnel you can more or less coast the last 25 miles into North Bend. The guys at the shop were pumped for us and put the first round on the house, and sitting out back with a beer after four days of dust felt amazing.

What I’d do differently. Camp on the Beverly side of the river, at Nunnally Lake or the dunes, and get dinner from the gas station. Vantage has a hot meal but it adds miles in both directions. Bring wider tires if you have the choice. And check which days the shuttle runs.

So which one?

If you have never done this, do Pittsburgh to DC. It is flat, it is well traveled, and you can’t get lost. If you want to find out how many miles you have in you, the Route Verte will tell you, politely and in French. If you want a story, go to Washington and ride east until the trees stop.

On value, it is hard to beat. The trails themselves are free. The money goes to getting there, burgers, beer, and in one case a very large Uber.

If you have questions about any of these, let me know. I’m happy to get into routes, where to stop, or what I’d pack differently.
